newsitem.title: USA: U.S. High Court broadens police traffic-stop power.
newsitem.headline: U.S. High Court broadens police traffic-stop power.

text.p: The Supreme Court ruled Wednesday that passengers can be asked by police during a routine traffic stop to leave the vehicle.
The high court, by a 7-2 vote, sided with the state of Maryland and with Attorney General Janet Reno, who had argued the case in December, in broadening police powers during traffic stops.

Chief Justice William Rehnquist said for the majority that the high court in 1977 held that a police officer may order the driver of a lawfully stopped car to exit the vehicle. He said the same powers now extend to passengers as well.

He rejected the argument that the constitutional protections against unreasonable searches and seizures prohibit police from ordering passengers out of cars during routine checks without grounds to suspect a crime has been committed.
Rehnquist cited the public interest in police safety and said the extra intrusion on the privacy interests of the passengers would be "minimal" by having them leave the car.

Justice John Paul Stevens dissented, saying: "How far this ground-breaking decision will take us, I do not venture to predict. I fear, however, that it may pose a more serious threat to individual liberty than the court realizes."
